correctness.rationale: For each admissible actuator direction, matching trace and determinant to \(\lambda^2\) gives the unique feedback products \(b_1k_1=a^2/(a-d)\) and \(b_2k_2=-d^2/(a-d)\). Cauchy--Schwarz gives the sharp feedback-norm minimum. The resulting closed-loop matrix is nonzero, rank one, and nilpotent, so its spectral and Frobenius norms coincide. A separate sharp square inequality gives the transient minimum at the same squared actuator weights. The rational witness and symbolic identities are replayed from the packaged checker.

evidence: The 1996 robust-deadbeat paper states that deadbeat closed-loop matrices are nilpotent and may have nontrivial Jordan structure, motivating a robustness objective beyond pole location.
The 2014 arbitrary-pole-placement paper explicitly defines the minimum-gain exact pole-placement problem as minimizing the feedback-matrix norm for prescribed poles.

The 2023 input-assignment/gain paper jointly designs input assignment and feedback gain, but its objective shifts one dominant eigenvalue while preserving the remaining eigenstructure rather than making the whole closed loop nilpotent.

originality.rationale: Minimum-gain minimum-time deadbeat control, robust deadbeat regulation, and minimum-gain exact pole placement are prior work. The closest inspected full sources optimize the feedback matrix for a fixed input matrix or optimize deadbeat robustness after the plant input matrix is fixed. A later joint input-assignment/gain paper solves a different one-mode eigenvalue-shift problem rather than nilpotent deadbeat placement. The 1988 minimum-gain deadbeat article was not available in full through the inspected routes and remains an explicit residual risk, but its indexed subject is controller gain for a given linear discrete-time system rather than actuator-direction co-design. Targeted semantic and exact-form searches found no source implying the common actuator optimizer, the sharp transient minimum, or the reciprocal modal-gap law.
residual_risks: The 1988 minimum-gain minimum-time deadbeat article was not available in full through the inspected routes and could contain a low-dimensional specialization not visible in indexing records.
Older eigenstructure-assignment literature may express actuator-direction co-design through an equivalent input-coordinate parametrization not captured by the search terminology.

The simultaneous transient optimum is proved only for two orthogonal modes and one scalar actuator; broader co-design literature may contain higher-dimensional results whose special cases were not stated explicitly.

value.rationale: Deadbeat pole placement trades settling time against gain and transient robustness. The theorem resolves the first nontrivial actuator-direction co-design exactly: it shows that gain and one-step transient objectives unexpectedly have the same actuator optimizer, while proving that neither can prevent reciprocal-gap blow-up as stable modes coalesce. The exact stable-plant witness has a first-step amplification \(24/5\) despite zero closed-loop poles and minimum gain within the actuator class, making the boundary directly relevant to robust pole-placement intuition.
